{"ghsa_id":"GHSA-32h6-97mm-8q3c","cve_id":null,"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security-advisories/GHSA-32h6-97mm-8q3c","html_url":"https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-32h6-97mm-8q3c","summary":"Wasmtime component async-lifted callback result count is unvalidated, causing a native stack buffer overflow","description":"## Impact

Wasmtime contained a bug where it did not properly validate the return types of core functions used as component-model-async callback function, which in combination with how the runtime works can allow the guest to write up to ~16KB of arbitrary data of its choosing to the process's native stack.  Since the guest is able to write data of its choosing to the native stack, it is able to overwrite return addresses, which can then be used to pass control to arbitrary host code or crash the process. While OS features like address space layout randomization and a non-executable stack can thwart simple attempts of arbitrary code execution, it's still recommended for embedders to treat this as if it's a arbitrary code execution sandbox escape vulnerability.  

Wasmtime relies on `wasmparser` to validate Wasm modules and components and ensure they adhere to the rules established in their respective specifications. That validation serves as a first line of defence against malformed and possibly malicious guest code. In addition, Wasmtime includes a variety of assertions, type checks, and bounds checks when translating Wasm code and compiling it to native code, as well as runtime checks for conditions which can't be verified statically, to ensure that the WebAssembly sandbox guarantees are preserved. However, in this case none of those mechanisms caught the invalid components:

- The logic for validating the type signature of the callback function used for async-lifted exports in `wasmparser` v0.259.0 and earlier was incorrect, accepting invalid components as valid instead of rejecting them. Specifically: instead of asserting that the function takes three `i32` parameters and returns a single `i32` result, due to a typographic error it asserted that the function must either accept three `i32` parameters or a single `i32` parameter without checking the result type(s) at all.

- When Wasmtime used `wasmparser` to parse a component and convert it into an internal representation, it recorded the index of each callback function without asserting that the return type and arity were correct, assuming `wasmparser` had already done that. Later, when the compiler generated a host-to-guest trampoline function for invoking the callback function, it did not include a runtime bounds check that the array reserved for passing the parameters and accepting the result was large enough for the target function signature, trusting instead that the caller knew the type of the callee and had allocated appropriately. Finally, when the runtime called the callback, it allocated a return area on the stack matching the expected arity rather than the actual one, again assuming that `wasmparser` would have already rejected the component had there been a mismatch.

In short, the soundness of runtime calls to guest callback functions depended crucially on `wasmparser` correctly rejecting invalid type signatures, and though additional defense-in-depth bounds checks could have caught the overflow at runtime, none were yet in place.

## Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.4 and 49.0.2 have been released with a fix for this issue.

## Workarounds

The issue can be avoided by disabling the `component-model-async` feature, in which case Wasmtime will reject components which use any async features, including async callbacks. Alternatively, embedders may use a patched version of `wasmparser` (v1.260.0 or later) to validate components and reject invalid ones prior to passing them to Wasmtime.

# Wasmtime component async-lifted callback result count is unvalidated, causing a native stack buffer overflow

This is an entry in the RustSec database for the Wasmtime security advisory
located at
https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-32h6-97mm-8q3c
For more information see the GitHub-hosted security advisory.

{"ghsa_id":"GHSA-cfhf-m2cr-62wj","cve_id":null,"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security-advisories/GHSA-cfhf-m2cr-62wj","html_url":"https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-cfhf-m2cr-62wj","summary":"Mis-typed WebAssembly tag imports can lead to GC heap corruption","description":"### Impact

Wasmtime contained a bug where validation of WebAssembly components which instantiate a core module importing a WebAssembly tag was not implemented correctly. This bug meant that Wasmtime could accept an invalid component which is not sound. Specifically modules were allowed to import tags with a subtype of the original tag's type, which is not allowed by the WebAssembly specification.

This bug then enabled guests to mis-type the payload of an exception object which can lead to GC heap corruption. Wasmtime's GC heap is implemented to be resilient to corruption but this is nevertheless a bug to fix. Wasmtime is not 100% bug-free in the face of a corrupt GC heap at this time hence this advisory being issues. Wasmtime may panic in certain operations when the GC heap is corrupt, so users are recommended to update.

This bug only affects users when the WebAssembly exceptions proposal is enabled, which is on-by-default starting in Wasmtime 47.0.0.

### Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.4 and 49.0.2 have been released which fix this validation error and correctly rejects ill-formed components.

### Workarounds

There is no known workaround for this issue at this time and it's recommended that users upgrade or change their embedding to disable the WebAssembly exceptions proposal.

### References
_Are there any links users can visit to find out more?_

{"ghsa_id":"GHSA-hw8m-q44c-ggrf","cve_id":null,"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security-advisories/GHSA-hw8m-q44c-ggrf","html_url":"https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-hw8m-q44c-ggrf","summary":"Rooting for GC values live across `try_call` may be missing, causing GC heap corruption","description":"## Impact

When compiling a Wasm module that uses GC references, a GC reference that is live across a `try_call` may, in certain conditions, not be properly rooted. If the callee causes a garbage collection, that reference may become stale or dangling, causing further issues including GC heap corruption or other incorrect execution.

Every Wasmtime version with GC and exceptions is affected by this issue. Both GC and exceptions are on-by-default in Wasmtime v47 and above.

## Patches

The fix is present in main and patch releases are made for 48.0.4 and 49.0.2.

## Workarounds

{"ghsa_id":"GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg","cve_id":null,"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security-advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg","html_url":"https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg","summary":"Filesystem sandbox escape when paths or symlinks contain trailing slashes","description":"## Impact

Wasmtime's filesystem implementation provided in the `wasmtime-wasi` crate contained a bug which allowed guests to escape their filesystem sandbox and read/write external files and directories. Guests provided write-access to any directory within their sandbox could then access any directory or file on the filesystem the host process could access, and guests provided read-only access to a directory in their sandbox might be able to read any contents on the filesystem depending on symlinks preexisting in the directory. This bug is a full filesystem sandbox escape for guests.

Wasmtime's filesystem sandboxing is primarily provided by the cap-std family of crates. This dependency had a vulnerability, [GHSA-hp8f-xmx4-4qrg](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/cap-std/security/advisories/GHSA-hp8f-xmx4-4qrg), which meant that when dealing with symlinks a trailing slash could be used in specific circumstances to escape the filesystem sandbox. This affects all published versions of Wasmtime at the time of this advisory's publication.

This specific bug within cap-std does not affect users using a Linux kernel after 5.6 with the `openat2` syscall. In this situation cap-std uses the `RESOLVE_BENEATH` flag which is not affected by this bug in cap-std. Users on macOS or older Linux kernels, however, are affected by this issue.

## Patches

Wasmtime 24.0.13, 36.0.14, 46.0.3, and 47.0.4 are being released with this advisory which patches this issue. The release 48.0.0 and after is not affected by this advisory.

## Workarounds

There is no known workaround for this issue. User are recommended to upgrade to a patch release of Wasmtime that contains a fixed version of `wasmtime-wasi`.

Wasmtime's implementation of WASIp3 contained a bug where the host would buffer a guest-specified-length buffer on the host without limit. This bug affects WASIp3 file and HTTP streams when writing. In both situations the host would unconditionally copy all of the bytes that a guest offered to the host and then buffer them up for processing. The size of this copy is not limited beyond the valid limits of the guest's linear memory.

This advisory is similar to a [previous advisory in Wasmtime](https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w) and applies to new locations not previously covered there, notably WASIp3 implementations.

### Patches

This bug is fixed in Wasmtime 46.0.3 and 47.0.4. WASIp3 notably was not enabled by default in Wasmtime versions prior to 46.0.0.

### Workarounds

There is no known workaround to this and users are recommended to upgrade.

{"ghsa_id":"GHSA-jqpg-j7w6-42pr","cve_id":null,"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security-advisories/GHSA-jqpg-j7w6-42pr","html_url":"https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-jqpg-j7w6-42pr","summary":"Dynamic record lifting can allocate beyond the hostcall fuel limit","description":"### Impact

Wasmtime's implementation of the dynamically-typed [`Val`] API does not adequately account for the amount of host allocations performed when loading a value from a guest. This means that a guest can return a value which allocates significantly more memory on the host than the host is otherwise keeping track of. This is a hole in the mitigations applied as part of GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w and represents a possible denial-of-service vulnerability for hosts.

This vulnerability only affects the [`Val`] API of hosts. Hosts that use `bindgen!` and otherwise statically-typed APIs are unaffected by this issue. For hosts using [`Val`] the amount of extra memory that can be allocated on the host depends on the exact shape of the API in question but it can be at least ~100x extra memory, for example.

### Patches

Wasmtime 36.0.16, 48.0.3, and 49.0.1 have been patched for this issue. 

### Workarounds

There is no known workaround to this and users are recommended to upgrade.

### References

* [`Val` API][`Val`]
* GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w

{"ghsa_id":"GHSA-m63x-6p34-q65x","cve_id":null,"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security-advisories/GHSA-m63x-6p34-q65x","html_url":"https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-m63x-6p34-q65x","summary":"`call_ref` and exception `catch` can drop some fuel accounting, leading to exponential fuel amplification","description":"## Impact

When compiling with the Cranelift backend, Wasmtime's fuel accounting around `call_ref` callsites, and also around the catch (exceptional) path for calls within `try_table`s, can drop any accumulated fuel usage within the callee, resetting to the fuel-remaining before the call. This can lead to exponential fuel amplification, that is, a guest that can run for exponential time using linear fuel, effectively avoiding timeouts or regular periodic yields. This is thus a denial-of-service vulnerability in Wasmtime.

The bug requires the use of fuel (`Config::consume_fuel` or `-W fuel=N` in wasmtime-cli), which is off by default. If fuel is enabled the bug affects any configuration using Cranelift, which is the default unless Winch has been configured, and includes users of the Pulley interpreter.

The bug only affects guests that have the `call_ref` or `try_table` opcodes present. The `call_ref` opcode is part of the function-references proposal to WebAssembly, the `try_table` opcode is part of the exception-handling proposal to WebAssembly, and users can also check if they are affected in specific cases by scanning guest bytecode for either opcode. The bug is present in all versions of Wasmtime that support `call_ref`, `try_table` and fuel. `call_ref` and `try_table` have been supported by default since Wasmtime 47.0.0. 

## Patches

Wasmtime 48.0.3 and 49.0.1 have been released with fixes for this issue.

## Workarounds

Wasmtime embedders that only require periodic interruption may consider the use of epoch interruption (`Config::epoch_interruption`) instead. Epoch interruption is not deterministic as fuel is; if deterministic fuel consumption metering is required, the only workaround is an upgrade to a fixed version of {"ghsa_id":"GHSA-hgjw-h833-99q9","cve_id":null,"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security-advisories/GHSA-hgjw-h833-99q9","html_url":"https://github.com/bytecodealliance/wasmtime/security/advisories/GHSA-hgjw-h833-99q9","summary":"Stores can mix up type indices between engines","description":"## Impact

Several public Wasmtime APIs allowed putting an object belonging to `Engine` B into a `Store` belonging to `Engine` A, after which internal lookups that key on raw unique-per-engine indices silently returned the wrong answer.

This bug is ***not triggerable by guest WebAssembly programs***. It requires the embedder to create two `Engine`s and mix objects between them. The `wasmtime` CLI is not affected.

The most serious consequence is a potential out-of-bounds write. Wasmtime could accidentally use a trampoline compiled for one signature with a Wasm function of a different signature. The trampoline stack allocates space for values passed between Wasm and the host, sized based on the function's signature, and then the host writes its return values past the end of the stack allocation.

The affected entry points:

* `Instance::new`, `Instance::new_async`, `InstancePre::instantiate`, and `InstancePre::instantiate_async`: These methods did not check that the given `Module` was associated with the `Store`'s `Engine` until *after* they had already registered the `Module`'s code in the `Store`, leading to potential trampoline mismatches.
* `Store::debug_register_module`, `Store::debug_register_component`, `BreakpointEdit::add_breakpoint`, and `BreakpointEdit::remove_breakpoint`: These methods failed to check that their given `Module` or `Component` was associated with the `Store`'s `Engine`, leading to potential trampoline mismatches.
* `StructRefPre::new`, `ArrayRefPre::new`, and `ExnRefPre::new`: These methods failed to check that their given type came from the same `Engine` as their `Store`, resulting in potential GC heap corruption (sandboxed within the GC heap).
* `Tag::new`: This method did not check that its given `TagType` came from the same `Engine` as its `Store`, leading to type confusion and/or panicking.

## Patches

Every public API that takes a `Store` now correctly validates the engine. Functions that returned `Result`s return an `Err(...)` when given an object from the wrong `Engine`; functions that do not return a `Result` panic when given such an object. Wasmtime versions 24.0.12, 36.0.13, 46.0.2, and 47.0.3  have these fixes.

## Workarounds

Wasmtime embedders are highly encouraged to upgrade their `wasmtime` crate dependency. Embedders using a single `Engine` for the lifetime of the process are not affected. Embedders not directly calling one of the affected methods are not affected.

If upgrading is not an option, ensure every object handed to a `Store` was created by that store's `Engine`, for example:

```rust
use wasmtime::{Engine, Instance, Module, Result, Store, ensure};

fn instantiate<T>(store: &mut Store<T>, module: &Module) -> Result<Instance> {
    ensure!(
        Engine::same(store.engine(), module.engine()),
        "module comes from a different engine than the store",
    );
    Instance::new(store, module, &[])
}
